summary: The people standing in the town: merchants, guards, the blacksmith. Cloth, skin and leather on a figure seen from a few metres.
why: A new profile rather than borrowing one, because an NPC is not quite either of the two
it sits between.
It is not world. Scenery is tiling art on large flat faces seen at a distance, upscaled
with the drawn model at full strength and padded by wrapping; an NPC's sheet is a figure
laid out on a page, does not tile, and wraps into nonsense at its edges.
It is not armour either, though it is close and shares its numbers. What differs is the
default material: an unnamed slot on a worn part is plate steel, because a worn part that
did not say is almost always armour. An unnamed slot on a townsperson is skin, because
a townsperson's sheet almost always carries a face - and getting that wrong makes a
barmaid's cheek a woven fabric.
The detail at 0.65 is armour's and is the point of the whole profile. These are painted
figures looked at from a few metres, where the drawn model at full strength turns folds
in cloth into hard-edged rectangles; the same setting protects a sword hilt for the same
reason.
Skin rather than cloth, and the reason is grain. cloth declares a weave along u at scale
140, which is right for a banner and wrong for a person: MU paints a townsperson's face
and her dress on one 128-pixel sheet, so a material chosen for the dress is also the
material on the face. Amy came out with fabric weave running down her cheek.
skin declares no grain at all, which is the safe way to be wrong here. A dress that has
lost a weave nobody could resolve at this size costs nothing; a face wearing one is the
first thing anybody notices.
